state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Well, it seems like you may be confusing alternate angles with angles that are always equal. In this case, alternate angles are not always equal. Let's go through the definition of alternate angles and why angles \( p \) and \( q \) are not necessarily equal in this scenario. Can you explain to me what alternate angles are and how they relate to the angles in the figure you provided?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so alternate angles are like... angles that are on opposite sides of the line crossing through, right? But I'm confused because I thought that meant they were always equal - like, isn't that the whole point of them being alternate? So are you saying they're only equal sometimes?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's a common misconception, but not all alternate angles are equal. Remember that alternate angles are formed when a transversal intersects two lines, and they are always on opposite sides of the transversal. In this case, angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate angles because they are on opposite sides of the transversal, but they are not necessarily equal. Can you think of a situation where alternate angles would be equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it now... so alternate angles are only equal when the two lines are parallel, right? But in this problem the lines aren't parallel, so that's why p and q aren't equal even though they're on opposite sides?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the misconception that alternate angles are always equal, uses appropriate questioning to guide discovery of the parallel lines condition, and the student successfully articulates the correct understanding by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher relies heavily on Socratic questioning rather than direct explanation with worked examples, which is inconsistent with the traditional strategy of explaining concepts directly and providing clear worked examples upfront.
